title: Polymer clay sculpted cat brooch
subtitle: A hand-sculpted sitting cat in polymer clay with detailed face markings, baked in a domestic oven
excerpt: A sitting cat brooch is a hand-sculpted polymer clay figure shaped from a single body piece with separately attached head details, baked in a domestic oven at 110-130°C. No kiln is required. The finished brooch is 4 cm tall and fitted with a brooch pin bar after baking.
sourceNotes: Technique derived from first principles for polymer clay sculpture jewellery.

glossaryTerms.definition: A PVC-based modelling clay that sets hard in a domestic oven at 110-130°C; decorative only, not food-safe
Warming and kneading polymer clay by hand until soft and pliable, preventing brittleness and cracking after baking

content.text: A sitting cat brooch is a flat-backed
polymer clay

figure built from a teardrop body, a round head, two pointed ears, a curled tail, and four short legs. The face details are scratched on with a needle tool and painted with acrylics after baking. The finished brooch is 4 cm tall and worn on clothing with a glued pin bar on the back.

materials.name: Polymer clay, main body colour (black, grey, orange, or cream)
Polymer clay, contrast colour for inner ear or face detail (optional)
Brooch pin bar with flat pad, 25 mm
Strong adhesive (epoxy or superglue, for attaching the pin bar after baking)
Acrylic paint for face detail (black, white)

tools.name: Fine liner brush (for painting face markings)

content.text: Preparation

Polymer clay bonds to itself through pressure in the raw state, so pieces can be attached and blended without any glue before baking. The flat back of the brooch is the working surface: build all pieces against a flat tile or piece of baking parchment so the back stays flush. This makes it easier to glue the brooch pin bar after baking.
Conditioning
Condition
all clay before use. Take 25 g of your main colour and knead between your palms for two minutes. The clay is ready when it stretches without tearing and feels smooth and warm throughout.
Shaping the body and tail

Take 12 g of conditioned clay and roll into a smooth oval. Place it on the baking parchment and flatten the back slightly so it lies flush. This is the cat body: compact and rounded, about 3 cm tall and 2 cm wide.
Roll a thin snake 8 cm long and 5 mm in diameter for the tail. Curl it around the base of the body in a C-shape, pressing the base of the tail against the body so it stays in place during baking.
This is a flat-backed
polymer clay

brooch. Build from a teardrop body, a round head, two ears, a curled tail, and four short legs. Scratch the face details with a needle tool. Paint them with acrylics after baking. The brooch is 4 cm tall. Glue a pin bar to the back.
Shaping the head
Take 7 g of conditioned clay and roll into a smooth sphere 2 cm in diameter. Flatten the back lightly so it sits flush against the top of the body.

Press the head to the top of the body and blend the neck join with a wooden rib. A cat's head sits forward of centre on the body: position it slightly toward the front of the brooch rather than dead centre.

Roll two small triangles for the ears, each from a 1 g piece of clay: pinch the triangle into a sharp point at the top and flatten the base. Press each ear to the top of the head on either side, angling them slightly outward. Blend the base of each ear into the head with a wooden rib.
Optional inner ear detail: press a tiny flat triangle of contrasting clay (pale pink or white) into the face of each ear triangle. Blend the edges slightly but leave the centre raised.
Adding legs and face markings

Roll four small sausages from the remaining clay, each about 2 cm long and 5 mm in diameter, for the front paws. Press two at the base of the body on either side, slightly tucked under the body curve. Blend the tops into the body.
Press the two rear paws behind the front paws, angling slightly outward. They should just peek out from behind the body base at each side.
Use the needle tool to scratch two almond-shaped eye indentations in the face, set 8 mm apart and 6 mm from the top of the head. The indentations will hold paint after baking.
Scratch a small V-shape for the nose and three fine lines on each side of the nose for whisker marks. These are texture marks, not cut-through lines: 0.5 mm depth is enough.
Baking

Place the brooch on its baking parchment on a small oven tray. Bake at 110-130°C (conventional oven, not fan) for 30 minutes. Allow to cool completely in the oven with the door slightly open before touching. The brooch is fragile when hot.
Finishing

Once cool, paint the face details with a fine liner brush and black acrylic paint: fill the eye indentations with solid black, then add a white highlight dot to the upper inside of each eye once the black is dry. Paint the whisker lines with a thin black line. Paint any stripe markings on the body if desired. Allow to dry fully, then apply a coat of matte or satin acrylic varnish over the entire piece. Glue a brooch pin bar to the flat back with epoxy or superglue. Allow the adhesive to cure for the time stated on the packet before wearing.
Care

Polymer clay brooches are durable but not indestructible. Do not drop on hard floors. Keep away from direct heat and sunlight, which can soften the clay. The pin bar bond is stronger with epoxy than with superglue over time: replace if the bar loosens. The finished piece is decorative jewellery, not food-safe.
Variations

Make a tabby cat by rolling thin ropes of a contrasting colour and pressing them against the body before assembly. Flatten them into the surface with a wooden rib so they read as stripes rather than raised ridges.
Turn the figure into a magnet instead of a brooch by gluing a small neodymium disc magnet to the flat back after baking. Keep magnets away from credit cards and electronics.

Make a matching set in miniature at half scale: use 12 g of clay total and roll all pieces proportionally smaller. The detail work at this scale is more challenging but the result is a dainty 2 cm brooch suitable for pinning to a lapel or hat.

items.problem: Head or ear fell off during baking
items.cause: The join was not pressed firmly enough in the raw state; polymer clay bonds through pressure alone
items.fix: After baking, reattach the piece with liquid polymer clay. Brush it onto both surfaces. Press the pieces together firmly. Re-bake for 15 minutes at the same temperature.

items.problem: Flat back not flat: the brooch rocks when laid down
items.cause: The clay was built up on the parchment but pieces added at the sides lifted the base off the flat surface
items.fix: While still raw, press the entire brooch gently down against the parchment to re-flatten the back. Place a small flat book on top and leave for 10 minutes before baking

items.problem: Acrylic paint peeled off after varnishing
items.cause: Paint was applied before the baked piece was fully cool, or varnish was incompatible with the paint
items.fix: Allow the piece to cool for at least one hour before painting. Use a water-based acrylic varnish over water-based acrylic paint. Solvent-based varnishes can lift water-based paint

items.cause: The clay was too soft when the indentations were scratched, and they closed up again
items.fix: Refrigerate the assembled brooch for 15 minutes before adding scratched detail. Cold clay holds surface marks better. Scratch more firmly and check the marks are clearly visible before baking
